title: Yield Criteria: Von Mises vs Tresca
text:
In 1d a typical stress-strain figure looks like the following:

This is what experimentalists get when doing a tensile test. After a certain stress \(\sigma_Y\), the behavior of the material is no longer purely elastic and the stress is no longer linearly dependent on the strain. The issue is that in a real material, we do not have uniaxial displacements and stresses, so the stress is a \(3 \times 3\) tensor, but at which stress does it yield? This is where equivalent stress come into play, we use a scalar \(\sigma_{eq} = f(\boldsymbol{\sigma})\) and compare it to the yield stress \(\sigma_Y\) to determine if plastic deformation happen. There are a variety of equivalent stress measures that we can choose, but in this course we consider the Von-Mises and Tresca equivalent stress.
The Von-Mises equivalent stress measures (1.35 in the lecture notes):
\[
\sigma_{eM}(\sigma_{ij}) = \sqrt{\frac{3}{2}\sigma_{ij}^\text{dev}\sigma_{ij}^\text{dev}}
\]
One thing that should be noted is that this is a scalar value, and it is an invariant of the stress tensor, meaning that the Von-Mises stress is independent on the basis in which we express the components of the stress tensors. We will see in exercise 5 that the Von-Mises stress can be written in term of principal stress:
\[
\sigma_{vM} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{2}\left[(\sigma_1-\sigma_2)^2 + (\sigma_2-\sigma_3)^2 + (\sigma_3-\sigma_1)^2\right]}
\]
We also defined the Tresca criterion. \[
\sigma_{\text{Tresca}} = \max\big(|\sigma_1-\sigma_2|,\ |\sigma_2-\sigma_3|,\ |\sigma_3-\sigma_1|\big) = \sigma_{max} - \sigma_{min}
\]
In the following cell, you can play around the two criterion and see when they differ.



Deviatoric plane σ₁+σ₂+σ₃ = const, projected orthogonal to the hydrostatic axis (1,1,1)

        σ₃ 0
        
      
      
      
        σ_y 200
        
      

      
        Uniaxial tension
        Uniaxial compression
        Pure shear
        Equibiaxial
        Mixed
      

      
        σ_m (hydrostatic)
        σ_vm (Von Mises)
        σ_tresca (σ_max−σ_min)

    The two criteria always agree exactly at the hexagon's corners (uniaxial-like states, where two
    principal stresses coincide) and diverge most at the corners' midpoints (pure-shear-like states),
    where Tresca is more conservative by a factor of 2/√3 ≈ 1.155. Motion purely along the hydrostatic
    axis (σ₁=σ₂=σ₃) doesn't move the point in this plane at all — both criteria are pressure-independent.
  




The two criteria always agree at the hexagon’s corners and diverge most at the edge midpoints (pure-shear states), where Tresca is more conservative by \(2/\sqrt{3}\approx1.155\).

title: Deviatoric / Spherical Decomposition
text:
Consider either the stress or the strain tensor. They can be decomposed into its spherical and volumetric part (Lecture notes 1.15 and 1.16).
\[
\sigma_{ij} = \sigma_{ij}^{\text{sph}} + \sigma_{ij}^{\text{dev}}
\]
where \(\sigma_{ij}^{\text{sph}} = \frac{1}{3} \sigma_{kk} \delta_{ij}\) is called the spherical part of the tensor. The deviatoric part is then given by
\[
\sigma_{ij}^{\text{dev}} = \sigma_{ij} - \sigma_{ij}^{\text{sph}} = \sigma_{ij} - \frac{1}{3} \sigma_{kk} \delta_{ij}
\]
In matrix notation:
\[
\boldsymbol{\sigma} =
\begin{pmatrix}
\sigma_{11} & \sigma_{12} & \sigma_{13} \\
\sigma_{21} & \sigma_{22} & \sigma_{23} \\
\sigma_{31} & \sigma_{32} & \sigma_{33}
\end{pmatrix}
\]
\[
\sigma_m = \frac{1}{3}\,\text{tr}(\boldsymbol{\sigma}) = \frac{1}{3}\left(\sigma_{11}+\sigma_{22}+\sigma_{33}\right)
\]
\[
\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{sph} = \sigma_m \, \mathbf{I} =
\begin{pmatrix}
\sigma_m & 0 & 0 \\
0 & \sigma_m & 0 \\
0 & 0 & \sigma_m
\end{pmatrix}
\]
\[
\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{dev} = \boldsymbol{\sigma} - \sigma_m \, \mathbf{I} =
\begin{pmatrix}
\sigma_{11}-\sigma_m & \sigma_{12} & \sigma_{13} \\
\sigma_{21} & \sigma_{22}-\sigma_m & \sigma_{23} \\
\sigma_{31} & \sigma_{32} & \sigma_{33}-\sigma_m
\end{pmatrix}
\]
Remark: What is the trace of a deviatoric tensor? Calculate it!


The following interactive illustration computes the deviatoric part and spherical part of the strain (in 2d). Starting from a square, the deformation due to the spherical and deviatoric part of the tensor are shown. Keep the values for \(\epsilon_{11}, \epsilon_{12}\), and \(\epsilon_{22}\) relatively low. What happens to the shape and the deformed area under deviatoric and spherical strain? Push the values for the deformation higher, does it still hold?

The area change is due to the spherical part and the deviatoric part deforms the solid but keeps the area constant. But this only holds for infinitesimal deformation!




ε = εsph + εdev — drag the sliders to set ε₁₁, ε₂₂, ε₁₂

  
    
      ε₁₁ 0.18
      
    
    
      ε₂₂ -0.06
      
    
    
      ε₁₂ = ε₂₁ 0.10
      
    
  

  
    Pure dilation
    Pure deviatoric (uniaxial)
    Pure shear
    Mixed
    Reset to zero
  

  
    
      
      εsph = εv I — area change, no shape change
      
      
    
    
      
      εdev = ε − εv I — shape change, tr = 0
      
      
    
    
      
      ε = εsph + εdev
      
      
    
  

  
    
      ε
      
    
    
      εsph = εvI, εv = ½tr(ε)

    Squares are drawn with the finite map x′ = (I + ε)x for visual clarity, not the strict
    infinitesimal linearization — so at large strain the "area-preserving" property of the
    deviatoric part is only approximate (visible as small drift in the reported areas).

title: Elastic Constants: E, ν, λ, μ
section: Poisson’s ratio — what does it mean?
text:
Poisson’s ratio — what does it mean?
Pull a bar and it usually gets thinner — that lateral response is set by \(\nu\). Try the presets below: cork (\(\nu\approx0\)), typical metals (\(\nu\approx0.3\)), rubber (\(\nu\approx0.499\), nearly incompressible), and auxetic foam (\(\nu<0\), gets fatter when stretched).



Pull a bar along its length — ν sets how much it shrinks (or grows) sideways

  
    
      Applied axial strain ε 0.20
      
    
    
      Poisson's ratio ν 0.30
      
    
  

  
    Typical metal (ν≈0.30)
    Cork (ν≈0.00)
    Rubber (ν≈0.499)
    Perfectly incompressible (ν=0.5)
    Auxetic foam (ν≈−0.5)
  

  
    
    
      Lateral strain ε_lat = −νε
      Length change
      Width change
      Volume change ΔV/V₀
    
  

  
    Pull most ordinary materials and they get thinner as they get longer — that's a positive
    Poisson's ratio. ν=0 means no lateral response at all (like cork, which is why it's easy to push
    into a bottle without swelling out the sides). ν=0.5 means the material can't change volume — it
    must get thinner by exactly the amount needed to conserve volume (rubber, most fluids). Negative ν
    ("auxetic") materials do the opposite of intuition: pull them and they get fatter, not thinner.

title: Elastic Constants: E, ν, λ, μ
text:
Lamé constants ↔︎ (E, ν)
\[
\mu = \frac{E}{2(1+\nu)}, \qquad \lambda = \frac{E\nu}{(1+\nu)(1-2\nu)}, \qquad K = \frac{E}{3(1-2\nu)}
\]



Live isotropic elasticity conversion and 6×6 Voigt stiffness matrix (order 11,22,33,23,13,12)

  
    
      E (Young's modulus) 70 GPa
      
    
    
      ν (Poisson's ratio) 0.33
      
    
  

  Approaching the incompressible limit (ν → 0.5): λ and K diverge. Common for rubber-like materials; not physical for most metals/alloys.

  
    
      DERIVED CONSTANTS
      
        λ (Lamé's first parameter)
        μ = G (shear modulus)
        K (bulk modulus)
      
      
        μ = E / [2(1+ν)]  ·  λ = Eν / [(1+ν)(1−2ν)]  ·  K = E / [3(1−2ν)] = λ + 2μ/3
      

      λ(ν) AT FIXED E — SINGULARITY AT ν=0.5
      
    

    
      ISOTROPIC STIFFNESS MATRIX C (VOIGT)
      
    
  

  
    C relates Voigt stress and (engineering-shear) strain vectors: σ_V = C·ε_V, with the diagonal shear
    terms equal to μ (not 2μ) because γ_ij = 2ε_ij already carries the factor of two. Off-diagonal 4-5-6
    blocks are zero for an isotropic material — normal and shear response never couple.

title: Elastic Constants: E, ν, λ, μ
section: What do λ and μ mean physically?
text:
What do λ and μ mean physically?
\(\mu\) resists pure shape change (shear). \(\lambda\) is subtler — it’s the stress that appears sideways only when lateral strain is prevented (confined loading), not something you’d feel in a free pull test.



μ resists shape change; λ is the stress that shows up sideways when shape change is prevented

  
    
      μ (shear modulus) 40 GPa
      
    
    
      λ (Lamé's 1st parameter) 60 GPa
      
    
  

  
    
      μ — resistance to shape change
      Apply a shear strain γ; τ = μγ is the stress needed to hold it there
      
      
        Shear strain γ 0.25
        
      
      τ = μγ = 
    

    
      λ — sideways stress when confined
      Squeeze/stretch a bar between rigid walls (ε_lateral locked at 0)
      
      
        Axial strain ε 0.15
        
      
      σ_axial = (λ+2μ)ε = σ_wall = λε = 
    
  

  
    Left: shear an element with the walls free to move — no volume or lateral coupling involved, just μ
    fighting the change of angle. Right: pull/push a bar but clamp its sides so it can't bulge or
    neck sideways (ε_lateral = 0 by construction, not by Poisson relaxation) — the walls still feel a
    push or pull, and that reaction is exactly λε. λ isn't a "stiffness" you can feel directly in an
    unconstrained pull test (that's E); it only shows up once something stops the material from doing
    what its Poisson's ratio would otherwise let it do. Note λ+2μ = M, the constrained (uniaxial-strain)
    modulus — the same quantity that sets P-wave speed in geomechanics/seismology.
